record.paper_title: Dense ideals in topological algebras: some results and open problems
record.original_question: Suppose a topological algebra A has a dense finitely generated ideal I = x1 A + · · · + xn A. Must A contain a proper topologically invertible element? More strongly, must the ideal I itself contain a topologically invertible element?

evidence.quote: The proper topologically invertible elements are defined as elements of Gt(A) \ G(A).

Problem 6. Suppose that a topological algebra has a dense, finitely generated ideal I = x1A + · · · + xnA. Does it follow that A has proper topologically invertible elements ? We can ask also a stronger question, whether the ideal I must have a topologically invertible element.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a topological algebra over $\mathbb{C}$ with identity $e$ (i.e., a complex algebra equipped with a Hausdorff topology making the multiplication separately continuous). Denote by $G(A)$ the group of (two-sided) invertible elements of $A$. An element $x \in A$ is called topologically invertible if there exist nets $(a_\alpha), (b_\alpha)$ in $A$ such that $x a_\alpha \to e$ and $b_\alpha x \to e$; let $G_t(A)$ denote the set of topologically invertible elements. An element of $G_t(A) \setminus G(A)$ is called a proper topologically invertible element.

Suppose that $A$ contains a dense, finitely generated right ideal
$$ I = x_1 A + x_2 A + \cdots + x_n A, $$
with $I \neq A$ (i.e., $I$ is a proper but dense ideal).

(a) Must $A$ contain a proper topologically invertible element, i.e., is $G_t(A) \setminus G(A) \neq \emptyset$?

(b) More strongly, must the ideal $I$ itself contain a topologically invertible element?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the literature on dense ideals in topological algebras. A targeted web search did not reveal any subsequent paper resolving the question of whether the existence of a dense finitely generated ideal forces the existence of a proper topologically invertible element (or one inside the ideal). No solution was found, so the problem appears to remain open.
